Cesarean section pain

Three exact-category randomized trials reported lower immediate postoperative pain, and one recent trial also improved scar-healing scores. Medication-use findings were inconsistent, and the review could not pool earlier trials because their protocols and outcomes differed.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Three exact-category randomized trials reported lower immediate postoperative pain, and one recent trial also improved scar-healing scores. Medication-use findings were inconsistent, and the review could not pool earlier trials because their protocols and outcomes differed.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact cesarean-section category contains seven records: three completed randomized trials, one controlled nonrandomized study, one systematic review, and two trial protocols without results. The review summarizes four earlier randomized studies, including trials indexed under related postoperative-pain categories, and overlaps some primary reports. It is a secondary synthesis, not an additional trial. The clinical findings concern pain and incision healing during early recovery.

Human and clinical evidence

A randomized trial of 80 patients found lower pain ratings at several time points over the first 24 hours after laser treatment. Participants also used less analgesic medication on average and waited longer before their first request for medication (Poursalehan et al. 2018).

In a sham-controlled trial of 88 patients, the two active PBM groups had larger effects on pain ratings and pressure sensitivity than the placebo and control groups. The treatments were given at 12 and 24 hours after surgery (de Holanda Araujo et al. 2019).

A 2026 randomized study of 104 patients found a 1.4-point reduction in pain after the second application and improved overall scar-healing scores, including vascularity and pliability. It did not find a significant difference in the need for medication or global health perception (de Melo Trindade et al. 2026). A separate controlled nonrandomized study reported better recovery, but its description of methods and results is less clear (Dehghanpour et al. 2023).

The systematic review included four earlier trials with 473 women but did not pool pain results because laser parameters, comparators, follow-up, and outcome measures differed. It rated the overall certainty low to very low. The review also found wound-healing evidence limited and inconsistently measured (Boaviagem et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for post-cesarean pain or incision recovery was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The studies used red visible light at 650–660 nm, sometimes combined with 804-nm near-infrared light. The 2026 trial used 660 nm at 5 J/cm² and 120 mW, applying 42 seconds per point along the incision at two sessions 48 hours apart. The 2019 trial used two red-light doses at 12 and 24 hours; the 2018 study combined red and near-infrared light. Differences in dose, timing, comparator, and measurement limit selection of one preferred regimen.

Interpretation

Short-term pain decreased in all three exact-category randomized trials, and one newer trial also improved scar-quality measures. Medication use did not decrease in that recent trial, and the broader review found enough variation to prevent a pooled estimate. The results are most relevant to immediate postoperative recovery, not long-term scar or surgical outcomes.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low to moderate for short-term pain reduction after cesarean birth.

Low for consistent reduction in analgesic use or improved wound recovery.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Three exact-category randomized trials report lower immediate pain, and the 104-person trial also found better scar scores. This supports a low-to-moderate rating for those short-term outcomes. Medication use was not consistently reduced, and the review rated overall certainty low to very low because protocols differed. Larger harmonized trials would clarify the size and durability of benefit.
